title: Lab 5 Count Regression
text:
The NMES1988 dataset contains 4,406 respondents from the US National Medical Expenditure Survey. The outcome is the number of physician office visits. The predictors are number of chronic conditions, self-perceived health, gender, years of education, and private insurance coverage.
The reference groups are average for health, male for gender, and no for private insurance.

Figure 1: Distribution of physician office visits.





The outcome is a count of physician office visits, so it takes whole-number values starting at zero. About 15.5% of participants had no visits. Most people had few visits, but the chart has a long tail to the right, with a few high counts and a maximum of 89 visits. The variance (45.69) is much higher than the mean (5.77), so I’ll check whether the Poisson model can account for that much variation.

title: Lab 5 Count Regression
text:
Part 2. Specify competing count models

2.1. Why not a linear model?








Figure 2: DHARMa residual diagnostics for the Gaussian model.





Both DHARMa plots suggest that the Gaussian model fits the visit counts poorly. In the Q–Q plot, the black points curve away from the red diagonal, so the residuals look different from what we would expect with a good fit. In the right panel, the middle red curve stays below the middle dashed line, suggesting that the model tends to predict too many visits. The outer curves spread farther apart at higher predicted visit counts, and the stars mark observed counts higher than all the simulations for those people. This linear model assumes that the expected count changes by a fixed amount for each extra unit of a numeric predictor. It also assumes bell-shaped errors with the same spread at every prediction and can simulate negative values. The real visit counts are whole numbers starting at zero, with many low counts and a few very high ones.

Each test compares the model in that row with the model above it.











The comparison of the chronic model with the null model gave χ² = 2175.43 with 1 degree of freedom (p <0.001). The comparison of the full model with the chronic model gave χ² = 959.92 with 5 degrees of freedom (p <0.001).
The likelihood-ratio tests showed that adding chronic conditions improved the fit over the null model. Adding health, gender, schooling, and insurance improved the fit further. I chose M2 as the Poisson model to carry forward because it had the highest (least negative) log-likelihood, so it fit the observed visit counts best of the three models. M2 also had the lowest AIC and BIC, so it was still preferred after accounting for the extra predictors. I’ll check how well M2 fits the data in Part 3.

title: Lab 5 Count Regression
text:
Part 3. Evaluate the Poisson model

3.1. Simulate residuals








Figure 3: DHARMa residual diagnostics for the full Poisson model.







3.2. Test for overdispersion and excess zeros
The dispersion ratio was 7.25 (simulation p = 0). The ratio of observed to expected zeros was 14.91 (simulation p = 0). A simulation p-value displayed as zero means none of the 500 simulations was as extreme as the observed result.


3.3. Interpret the diagnostics
The Q–Q plot bends away from the diagonal, and residuals pile up near both ends of the right panel. This suggests the Poisson model struggles with very low and very high counts. The dispersion ratio was 7.25, and there were 14.91 times as many zeros as expected. Poisson assumes the variance equals the mean. With extra variation, its standard errors and p-values tend to be too small and its confidence intervals too narrow. I’ll check whether a negative binomial model’s extra spread can account for the zeros before adding a separate model for them.

title: Lab 5 Count Regression
section: Part 4. Fit and evaluate a negative binomial model
text:
Part 4. Fit and evaluate a negative binomial model

4.1. Estimate the NB2 model
The negative binomial model uses the same predictors as the full Poisson model.


4.2. Compare the Poisson and NB2 models
The likelihood-ratio test comparing NB2 with the full Poisson model gave χ² = 12,129.08 with 1 degree of freedom (p <0.001).
NB2 fits significantly better than the full Poisson model. The single degree of freedom comes from the extra parameter NB2 uses to estimate the spread of the counts. In the DHARMa plots below, the Q–Q points are closer to the diagonal, and the dispersion test suggests NB2 captures the overall spread. The Poisson model underestimated that spread, so its standard errors were likely too small. The red curves still bend, and NB2 still predicts too few zeros.


4.3. Re-check the NB2 model with DHARMa








Figure 4: DHARMa residual diagnostics for the negative binomial model.





The dispersion ratio was 1.05 (simulation p = 0.392). The ratio of observed to expected zeros was 1.10 (simulation p = 0.004).


4.4. Visualize predicted counts








Figure 5: Predicted mean visits by number of chronic conditions. The shaded band shows the confidence interval for the mean.





The predictions hold years of schooling at its mean and health, gender, and insurance at their reference levels. With the log link, each extra chronic condition raises predicted visits by the same percentage. That adds more visits when the predicted count is already higher, so the line curves upward.

title: Lab 5 Count Regression
section: Part 5. Decide whether the zeros need their own model
text:
Part 5. Decide whether the zeros need their own model

5.1. Compare models for the zeros
The NB2 model’s ratio of observed to expected zeros was 1.10 (simulation p = 0.004). Because NB2 still expected too few zeros, I fitted a zero-inflated NB model and a hurdle NB model, using the same predictors for the visit counts and for the zeros.
The likelihood-ratio test comparing ZINB with NB2 gave χ² = 143.14 with 7 degrees of freedom (p <0.001).

I used DHARMa to re-check the hurdle model, which had the lowest AIC and BIC.








Figure 6: DHARMa residual diagnostics for the hurdle negative binomial model.





The hurdle model’s dispersion ratio was 1.15 (simulation p = 0.008). Its ratio of observed to expected zeros was 0.998 (simulation p = 0.984).


5.2. Justify the model choice
I would carry forward the hurdle model. The zero-inflated model fit better than NB2, and the hurdle model had the lowest AIC and BIC of all three. It expected about 684 people with no visits, close to the 683 we observed. It still slightly underestimates how much visit counts vary.
